headline: China mulls buying banned Nvidia chips, experts worry about Nvidia's influence on Trump
summary: China is reportedly considering allowing major AI firms like Alibaba and ByteDance to acquire millions of Nvidia's banned chips, while critics express concern over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's growing influence on former President Trump's AI policy.
details: China is reportedly considering relaxing controls to allow major AI firms like Alibaba and ByteDance to import millions of Nvidia's banned RTX Pro 5500 chips over the next year. These gaming chips are expected to be repurposed for servers to power the country's most in-demand AI models.

This development occurs despite a recent summit between Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping, where AI regulation and export controls were not discussed. A fragile trade truce was only extended for two months, with analysts anticipating potential US controls that could trigger Chinese retaliation.

Amid these geopolitical tensions, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang appears to be gaining significant influence over Trump's AI policy. Critics are concerned that Nvidia's profit motivations may be steering Trump's thinking at a crucial time, potentially downplaying the risks of new AI technology.

Nvidia, already the world's most valuable company, stands to profit immensely if risks are minimized and both countries prioritize rapid AI development. A key goal for Nvidia since Trump took office has been to reopen the Chinese market, which was restricted during the Biden administration.

US export controls had reportedly cut Nvidia's share of China's advanced AI chip market from about 95 percent to zero. Trump was not initially an ally, tightening controls further and even banning exports of H200 chips to China, while also considering breaking up Nvidia to foster domestic competition.

However, after a dinner meeting at Mar-a-Lago, Trump stated he "learned the facts of life" and recognized Nvidia as an "amazing" AI leader. Subsequently, he lifted export controls on H200 chips, which China eventually allowed to be sold to some firms, despite warnings from lawmakers and national security experts.

Since then, Trump and Huang have frequently appeared together publicly and regularly communicate by phone, according to Stephen Witt, author of The Thinking Machine. Witt notes that Trump's recent claims, suggesting AI is a "hoax" that will be an economic boon, are "exactly Jensen's talking points."

Witt states that Jensen Huang is now the president's most influential advisor on technology issues, and the two have become quite close. He found that many hardware developers, like Huang, tend to have a very low sense of risk regarding AI technology, contrasting with software developers who urge the White House to take risks seriously.

This debate between the two camps has persisted for a decade without resolution. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed that Trump is "completely aligned with Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia," suggesting the president will continue to downplay AI risks and avoid serious talks with China on the matter.

headline_marked: [[Modal Labs nearing $750M round]] at $15.75B valuation, tripling in 4 months
headline: Modal Labs nearing $750M round at $15.75B valuation, tripling in 4 months
summary: The AI inference provider's valuation would more than triple from $4.65 billion just four months ago, highlighting soaring demand for AI model execution services.
details: AI inference infrastructure provider Modal Labs is reportedly nearing a $750 million funding round led by Accel. This deal would value the company at $15.75 billion, including the new investment, according to a source close to the funding.

This new valuation would more than triple Modal's previous valuation of $4.65 billion, which was set just four months ago during its $355 million fundraise. The rapid increase reflects intense investor interest in the AI inference sector.

The funding comes amid soaring demand for inference services, which involve running trained AI models to generate outputs, particularly for open-source models. Other inference startups like Baseten, Fireworks, and Fal are also in talks for significant capital infusions at much higher valuations.

Despite rapid revenue growth, these companies often face thin margins due to the high cost of acquiring or leasing compute resources. Fireworks, for instance, announced $1 billion in annualized revenue in July, a fivefold increase from the previous year.

Modal Labs was co-founded in 2021 by CEO Erik Bernhardsson and CTO Akshat Bubna. Bernhardsson previously built data teams at Spotify and Better.com, while Bubna was an early staff engineer at Scale AI.

Based in New York with approximately 150 employees, Modal allows developers to train AI models and run compute-heavy workloads without managing their own servers. Its customer base includes Cognition, Suno, Ramp, and Substack.
As of May, Modal had reportedly surpassed $300 million in annualized revenue. This growth underscores the critical role of inference providers in the expanding AI ecosystem.

The fundraising talks follow a security incident in late July where a customer's data was compromised. Modal stated the breach was due to a flaw in the customer's own code, not a compromise of Modal's platform.
